claude_summary: Idaho Code § 63-3024A sets the food tax credit (formerly the grocery credit) at $155 per person for tax year 2025 and each year after. The credit is refundable: any part above tax due is paid out as a refund. The household is one 56-year-old resident filer with no dependents. Nothing triggers proration: the head is not SNAP-eligible and no incarceration is listed. That gives $155. The engine awarded the full $155 base credit for all 12 months, which matches the law. The consensus answer of $0 rests on claims that the credit is nonrefundable, repealed or phased out, and all three are wrong. The 2026 bills that would have changed the credit (HB 605 and HB 633, which would have repealed it) were only printed and filed, so neither became law.

The household is one person, age 80 and disabled, with gross income of about $2,539 a month. In Jan–Feb 2026 that is above Arizona's 185% FPL expanded categorical eligibility limit, so the regular rules apply, and the net income and asset tests both deny benefits ($0). From March 2026 Arizona's limit is 200% FPL ($2,608.33 a month; $2,660 from October). The USDA BBCE table, updated 2026-06-29 (before the freeze), confirms 200% with no asset limit. That makes the household categorically eligible, which waives the income and resource tests. 7 U.S.C. 2017(a) and 7 CFR 273.10(e)(2)(ii)(C) then give the $24 FY2026 minimum benefit to every eligible one-person household, even though the benefit formula is negative. The engine's 10 × $24 = $240 matches this. Using $24 for Oct–Dec is right because the FY2027 COLA came out after the freeze. The $0 consensus applies 185% or the regular rules for the whole year.

Under A.R.S. §43-1072.01, a single filer who is not claimed as a dependent and has federal AGI of $12,500 or less gets $25 per resident person, capped at $100. Subsection D pays as a refund any amount above tax due. None of the Social Security is federally taxable: $6,808 of other income plus half of the benefits ($11,868) is $18,676, under the $25,000 base. Federal AGI is therefore about $6.7–6.8k, so this one-person unit gets $25. The engine's $25 matches this. Its AGI figure of $6,736 differs from stage 1's $6,808 only in how the $72 of non-Schedule D gains is handled, and that does not affect eligibility. The $0 consensus overlooks the credit or tests total income rather than federal AGI.

The law gives a single joint return with WV taxable income of $84,928: the spouse's $88,928 of wages less two $2,000 exemptions. The VA benefits are federally exempt, so they never enter AGI. SB 392 enacted W. Va. Code §11-21-4j, which cuts rates for tax year 2026 and was effective before the freeze. Under its schedule the tax is $1,950.50 + 4.58% × $24,928 = $3,092.19. The engine applied exactly these steps; its $88,927.65 AGI is float rounding. The consensus figure of $3,255.03 uses the superseded 2025 rates (2.22% to 4.82%).

claude_engine_step_at_issue: Arizona deductions of $15,750 subtracted from AGI $61,592.09 (standard deduction taken at the unindexed 2025 statutory amount rather than the 2026 inflation-adjusted amount required by A.R.S. 43-1041(H))
claude_summary: Arizona taxes at a flat 2.5% starting from federal AGI of $61,592. HB 4168 (Laws 2026, ch. 140, signed 2026-06-13) set the single standard deduction at $15,750, retroactive to tax year 2025. It kept subsection H, which says the department "shall adjust" that amount for inflation in the same way the federal basic standard deduction is adjusted. Indexed that way, the 2026 deduction is $16,100, the federal amount the IRS published on 2025-10-09. That gives taxable income of $45,492 and tax of $1,137.30. The engine applied the unindexed 2025 amount of $15,750, which produced $1,146.05. That is an engine defect. Stage 1 and the 12-model consensus both reached $1,137.30.

The head files single. AGI is $22,535: $17,443 wages, minus the $2,778 traditional 401(k), plus the $8,000 403(b) distribution, minus the $130 IRA deduction. The 2026 standard deduction of $16,100 leaves $6,435 of taxable income, and 10% of that is about $643.50. The engine took these same steps. Its $0.07 shortfall comes from carrying fractional inputs ($2,778.48 and $129.83), so the gap is negligible. No nonrefundable credit applies, which makes the consensus $0 wrong: §25B(d)(2) reduces Saver's Credit contributions by the $8,000 403(b) distribution received in the testing period, taking them to $0, and the AOTC is $0 because no qualified tuition is listed. Stage 1 stands.

claude_stage1_error: Stage 1 used the 2026 indexed parameters (3.4% CCPI, giving a $5,900 standard deduction, a $158 exemption credit and a $11,456 top for the 1% bracket). By its own account these were published after the 2026-07-03 reference-law freeze. Under the benchmark's frozen-law convention, the amounts governing tax year 2026 are the last ones the agency published before the freeze, the 2025 FTB figures ($5,706 / $153 / $11,079). Stage 1 itself showed that those figures reproduce the reference ($12.79). Its conclusion that the law supports the $0 consensus therefore rests on post-freeze amounts and should not stand. Its other findings were correct: no disability exemption credit under R&TC 17054, a $60 renter's credit under the 17053.5(k)(2) fallback, no medical itemization, and the disability exception to the early-distribution tax.
claude_summary: The head files single with CA AGI of about $22,535: wages of $17,443, less the $2,778 401(k) deferral, plus the $8,000 403(b) distribution, less the $130 IRA deduction. Medical costs fall below the 7.5% floor, so the standard deduction applies. Using the last amounts published before the 2026-07-03 freeze (the 2025 FTB figures: $5,706 standard deduction, $153 exemption credit, 1% bracket up to $11,079), tax is $225.79. Subtracting the $153 exemption credit and the $60 renter's credit (§17053.5(k)(2) falls back to $60 because the $250 enhancement was not funded) leaves $12.79. The engine followed exactly this path and got $12.78. The $0 consensus depends on the 2026 indexed amounts, which were not published until after the freeze, or on errors such as a nonexistent disability exemption credit or treating CalEITC as nonrefundable.

California's refundable credits for this single 28-year-old with no children come only from CalEITC. R&TC §17052 lets childless filers claim from age 18, and the §17052(o) extended phaseout runs to about $32,900 for 2025. Under IRC §32(a)(2)(B), the phaseout uses the greater of AGI ($22,535) or earned income. With the 2025 parameters, the latest published before the freeze, the credit is 0.85 × [0.0543 × ~$5,451 − ~1.0779% × (AGI − $5,451)] ≈ $95.15 at the FTB table midpoint, which matches the engine's $95.15. The engine counts earned income as $17,443 instead of $14,665 because it does not subtract the traditional 401(k) deferral, as §32(c)(2)(A)(i) requires. That does not change the result: both figures are past the phase-in, and AGI sets the phaseout. The $0 consensus applied the federal childless cutoff and missed the §17052(o) extension. The 2026 CCPI indexing (about 3.4%, giving roughly $105) was published only after the 2026-07-03 freeze, so the reference rests on law published before the freeze.

claude_engine_step_at_issue: Determining Ohio AGI of $94,925.30. The engine applied no R.C. 5747.01(A)(10)(b) deduction for unreimbursed medical care above 7.5% of federal AGI, even though the head's $6,500 of after-tax non-employer premiums plus $800 of other medical expenses exceed that threshold.
claude_summary: For 2026, R.C. 5747.02 sets Ohio's tax at $332 plus 2.75% of taxable income above $26,050. That base accounts for the consensus's whole $332 shortfall, so the consensus ($1,589.56) is wrong. The engine has the base, the two $1,900 exemptions and the $200 retirement income credit right. However, it starts from Ohio AGI equal to federal AGI ($94,925.30) and takes no medical-care deduction under R.C. 5747.01(A)(10)(b). On the stated facts the head paid $6,500 of non-employer insurance premiums and $800 of other medical costs, totaling $7,300. Premiums count as medical care under IRC 213(d)(1)(D), and $7,300 exceeds 7.5% of federal AGI ($7,119.38), so the deduction is about $180.63. Ohio tax after the retirement credit is then about $1,916.60, roughly $5 below the reference.

claude_engine_step_at_issue: The 'older child' step: the engine treated MAGI of 2.13× FPL as within NC's 211% limit for ages 6–18 (plus the 5-point disregard) without checking that the 133–211% band is the CHIP-funded optional targeted low-income child group (42 CFR 435.229), which excludes children covered under a group health plan. Child 1 has employer-sponsored insurance.
claude_summary: Child 1 is 11 and has employer-sponsored insurance all year. Federally, NC can cover children aged 6–18 only up to 133% FPL in the mandatory group under 42 CFR 435.118 (138% with the 5-point disregard), because its historical Medicaid level for that age group was no higher. The 133–211% band, the former NC Health Choice population, came into Medicaid in 2023 as Medicaid-expansion CHIP under the optional targeted low-income child group (42 CFR 435.229), and that group's definition in 42 CFR 435.4 excludes any child covered under a group health plan. The engine took MAGI of 2.13× FPL and tested it against the 211% older-child limit plus the disregard without looking at the child's coverage. With ESI, the 133% group is the only one that applies, and 213% FPL is above it, so Child 1 is not eligible (0), which matches stage 1 and the consensus.

claude_engine_step_at_issue: The OLDER_CHILD category check: the engine found Child 2 eligible because MAGI of 2.13× FPL is within NC's 211% (with disregard) children's limit. It did not apply the OTLIC / targeted low-income child rule that the 133–211% band for ages 6–18 excludes children covered under a group health plan. The input that Child 2 has employer-sponsored insurance was never used.
claude_summary: The law gives 0. Under federal law, NC Medicaid can cover children aged 6–18 between 133% and 211% FPL only through the CHIP-funded optional targeted low-income child (OTLIC) group, and that group excludes any child covered under a group health plan. The prompt states that Child 2 has employer-sponsored insurance, so the only group left is 435.118, capped at 133% FPL (138% with the 5-point disregard). Child 2's MAGI of $82,301 is about 212.8% of the 2026 FPL ($38,680 for 5), far above that cap. The engine tested only income against NC's 211% older-child limit and found eligibility, ignoring the no-other-coverage condition. So the reference of 1 misapplies the law, and the 44-model consensus of 0 is correct.

claude_stage1_error: Stage 1 (step 4) assumed the only Medicaid group that reaches 211% FPL for ages 6–18 is the Optional Targeted Low-Income Children group (42 CFR 435.229). That group requires no group health coverage, so stage 1 ruled Child 3 out over the employer coverage (step 5). Stage 1 missed that SPA 23-0009 also elected the "Individuals above 133% FPL under Age 65" group (42 CFR 435.218, SSA 1902(a)(10)(A)(ii)(XX)), with a 211% income standard. That group has no uninsured requirement, and it expressly picks up people who do not qualify for the other optional groups (435.218(b)(1)(iii)). So an insured 9-year-old at 207.8% FPL after the disregard qualifies, and stage 1's answer of 0 does not follow. Stage 1's income arithmetic was right (MAGI $82,301; 212.8% / 207.8% on the 2026 line), as was its April 1 timing caveat. That caveat leaves the child eligible April–December 2026, not ineligible for the year.
claude_summary: NC's SPA 23-0009 adopted two groups for children above the mandatory 133% standard, up to 211% FPL. One is the Optional Targeted Low-Income Children group, which excludes children with group health coverage. The other is the "Individuals above 133% FPL under Age 65" group (42 CFR 435.218), which has no insurance condition. So Child 3's employer coverage does not bar Medicaid. MAGI is $82,301 (wages $85,209, less the $2,778 traditional 401(k) and $130 IRA), which is 212.8% of the 2026 guideline ($38,680 for 5). After the 5% disregard that is 207.8%, within 211%. The engine (2.13x FPL against the 211% children's limit) matches the law, so the reference of 1 holds. One caveat: NC switches to the new guideline on April 1. For January–March, measured against the 2025 line, the child is at 213.6% and fails, so the child is eligible April–December.

Under 2026 law the couple files jointly with three children under 17, and their AGI is $82,301 ($85,209 in wages, minus $2,778 in traditional 401(k) deferrals, minus a $130 IRA deduction). Taxable income is $42,355: AGI minus the $32,200 standard deduction and the $7,746 §225 overtime deduction. Tax on that is $4,586.60, which is less than the $6,600 CTC, so $2,013.40 is refundable as ACTC (under both the $5,100 cap and the 15% earned-income limit). The EITC is $0 because AGI is above the $70,244 phase-out end. The engine got $2,013.49, all of it refundable CTC, and the $0.09 gap with stage 1 is immaterial rounding. Cluster 1's $0 leaves out the overtime deduction and/or uses the pre-OBBBA CTC. Cluster 2's $2,058.76 deducts the $378 of car-loan interest under §163(h)(4), but the facts that deduction requires (new vehicle, US final assembly, loan taken after 2024) are not listed, so the prompt treats them as false.

Connecticut's broad-based categorical eligibility, which CT calls Expanded Categorical Eligibility (ECE), covers this 2-person couple because their gross income of $2,536.25/mo is below 200% of the poverty line (about $3,525). CT DSS states that ECE households have no net income limit and need not meet the asset limit, and 7 CFR 273.8(a) and 273.9(a) waive the resource and income standards for categorically eligible households. So the $48,000 in savings and the net income above 100% of the poverty line do not disqualify the couple. Their formula benefit is $0, since 30% of net income exceeds the $546 maximum. But 7 CFR 273.10(e)(2)(ii)(C) gives every eligible 1–2 person household the minimum benefit of $24/mo (FY2026), so the annual amount is $288. That matches the engine and stage 1. The engine's net income ($2,118, against stage 1's $2,308) includes about $190 of extra deductions that stage 1 does not have, but this does not change the result: either figure makes the formula benefit $0.

The reference value of 0 is correct, but the engine narrative gives the wrong reason for it. Child 1 is 10 years old with household income of about $60,010 (MAGI) to $61,277, which is roughly 182–186% of the 2026 poverty guideline of $33,000 for a family of four. That clears PA's Medicaid limit of 133% for children aged 6–18 and falls within PA's CHIP income range (free up to 208%, low-cost up to 314%). Even so, the child is ineligible: federal Title XXI and 42 CFR 457.310 do not count a child covered by a group health plan as a targeted low-income child, PA DHS requires CHIP children to be 'Uninsured and not eligible for Medical Assistance', and the prompt says Child 1 has employer-sponsored insurance all year. The narrative says income is above PA's CHIP limit, which is wrong, since about 186% FPL is well under 314%. This may just be the narrative misdescribing the trace. It does not change the output on these facts, but the developer may want to confirm that the engine's PA CHIP income limit is set correctly.

Child 2 is 10 years old. Household MAGI is about $60,010, roughly 182% of the 2026 FPL for a household of four, so the child fails Pennsylvania's Medicaid income test but meets CHIP's age and income tests. However, the prompt says Child 2 has employer-sponsored insurance all year. Under 42 USC 1397jj(b)(1)(C), 42 CFR 457.310(b)(2) and Pennsylvania's own rule that the child be uninsured, that coverage means the child is not a targeted low-income child. The engine's output of 0 is therefore correct. The narrative's stated reason (failing an age or income threshold) looks like a misdescription of the trace, but the value matches the law. The 20-model consensus of 1 ignored the uninsured requirement.

Child 3 is 10. Household MAGI is $60,010, about 182% of the 2026 HHS guideline of $33,000 for a family of four. That is above Pennsylvania's Medicaid limit for children and within its CHIP income limit. The prompt says Child 3 has employer-sponsored insurance all year. Under 42 U.S.C. 1397jj(b)(1)(C) and 42 CFR 457.310(b)(2)(ii), a child covered by a group health plan is not a targeted low-income child, so Child 3 is not CHIP-eligible (0). The engine applied the same test as stage 1. The consensus models that answered 1 checked age and income only and skipped the no-other-coverage condition, which is a condition of eligibility, not of enrollment.

Act 45 of 2025 created Pennsylvania's Working Pennsylvanians Tax Credit, codified at Fiscal Code Art. XVI-W.2. The credit equals 10% of the federal EITC, is refundable, and applies to taxable years beginning after 12/31/2024, which includes 2026. This head of household has 3 qualifying children, $60,000 of earned income and $60,010 of AGI. Under the Rev. Proc. 2025-32 parameters (maximum credit $8,231, phase-out from $23,890 at 21.06%), the federal EITC is $624.13, so the WPTC is $62.41. The engine's steps match the law, and the consensus answer of $0 overlooks the new credit. The only possible difference is a few cents if the federal EITC is rounded to the IRS $50-bracket table (about $62.10).

Oklahoma expanded Medicaid, so the head, a 21-year-old who is not pregnant, not disabled and not on Medicare, falls in the expansion-adult group. That group uses a MAGI income test with no asset test, and having employer coverage does not bar eligibility. The head's MAGI is $312 of taxable interest. The $50,000 of 'financial assistance' is not a taxable source in IRC 36B MAGI. $312 is far below OHCA's 2026 limit for one person of $22,176 a year (effective 4/1/2026). The engine found MAGI of about $312 (0.02 times FPL) and adult-group eligibility, which matches the law. The consensus value of 0 rests on wrongly counting the $50,000 as income, applying an asset test, or saying Oklahoma did not expand.

Oklahoma's Sales Tax Relief Credit (68 O.S. § 5011; OAC 710:50-15-96) is refundable. It is $40 per allowable personal exemption when gross household income does not exceed $20,000 for a filer who has no dependents, is under 65 and is not disabled. Gross household income excludes gifts. The engine counted gross income of $312 (the taxable interest) and left out the $50,000 "financial assistance". It treated that amount as non-income help, which is the conventional meaning of the term (regular help from friends or relatives outside the household) and amounts to a gift. It then allowed $40 × 1 exemption. The Oklahoma EITC is $0 because the head has no earned income. On the most defensible reading of the facts the total is $40. The consensus answer of $0 depends on treating the assistance as public assistance, support money or scholarships, and the prompt's rules on benefit receipt and student status argue against that.

The law gives $288 ($24 a month for 12 months), which matches the engine. The household is the pregnant head alone. Countable income is $1,083.33 a month in wages plus $1,000 a month of financial assistance. Educational assistance is exempt under TWH A-1322.1. Gross income of $2,083.33 is above the 130% FPL limit but within Texas's 165% FPIL expanded categorical eligibility limit, and $190 in assets is under the TANF-NC limit, so the gross and net income tests are waived. Net income of $1,657.67 gives a formula benefit of $0 ($298 − $498), so an eligible one-person household gets the minimum benefit: 8% of $298, rounded to $24. The engine follows each of these steps and keeps the FY2026 amounts for October–December, which is right because the FY2027 COLA values came out after the 2026-07-03 freeze. The 33 models that answered $0 applied the 130% gross income test or the net income test, both of which categorical eligibility waives. The 3 that answered $1,208 dropped the $12,000 of financial assistance, which SNAP counts as income.

The household's income, $42,664, is about 156% of the poverty line. That puts it above the federal 130% free-meal limit, and with no SNP or TANF there is no categorical route, so on the federal tier alone the 6-year-old would get reduced-price meals. Minnesota law settles the question instead. Minn. Stat. § 124D.111, subd. 1c, requires schools in the National School Lunch Program to join the state free school meals program and to give every student one breakfast and one lunch per school day at no cost. Under subd. 1d, the state pays the gap up to the federal free rate. The engine set the meal tier to free through Minnesota's universal free school meals rule for the one K-12 child. That matches the law, so the reference of 1 holds. The consensus answer of 0 applied only the federal income test and missed the state program.

Under federal NSLP rules, this household's income ($42,664, about 156% of the 2026 poverty guideline for 3) would put the child in the reduced-price tier. However, Minn. Stat. 124D.111 subd. 1c requires every participating school to serve all students breakfast and lunch at no cost, and the state pays the gap up to the federal free rate. That makes the household's meal support free meals, which the output definition excludes. The engine assigned tier FREE under Minnesota's universal free meals and returned 0 for reduced-price support. This matches the law and the definition, and it agrees with stage 1's answer of 0. The derivation wrongly says 1.56 is 'above the reduced-price threshold' (it is below 1.85), but that slip does not change the result.

The spouse is 18, so they fall in Minnesota's Medical Assistance category for children under 19 (Minn. Stat. 256B.055 subd. 3a; 42 CFR 435.118). Its income limit is 275% FPG (256B.056 subd. 4; EPM 2.2.3.3). Neither the statute, the federal rule nor DHS's list of eligibility categories excludes married children, and MA-FCA has no asset test. The engine put the 3-person MAGI household at about 156% FPL ($42,664 against the 2026 guideline of $27,320) and found the spouse eligible under its older-child category. That matches the law, so the reference of 1 holds. The consensus answer of 0 wrongly applied the 133%/138% adult limit.

For 2026, Louisiana R.S. 47:297.8(A)(2) gives a credit of 5% of the federal EITC, and subsection (B) makes it refundable. The household files jointly with two qualifying children. Its earned income (wages plus self-employment income less half of SE tax, about $21,896) is above the $18,290 earned income amount and below the $31,160 joint phase-out threshold, so the federal EITC is the $7,316 maximum under Rev. Proc. 2025-32. 5% × $7,316 = $365.80, which is what the engine computed. The repeal bills (2025 SB 149 and HB 642, and 2026 HB 253, which would have repealed the income tax) were never enacted. No child care expenses are listed, so the other refundable Louisiana credits are $0. The consensus answer of 0 wrongly assumes Louisiana has no refundable EITC.

Under SSA §226 (42 U.S.C. 426), Head is entitled to Medicare at age 65 or older. Someone under 65 qualifies only after 24 calendar months of entitlement to disability-based Social Security benefits (SSDI, disabled adult child, or disabled widow(er)), or with ESRD or ALS. Head is 61 and flagged as disabled, but the prompt lists no disability benefits, no 24-month entitlement period, and no ESRD or ALS, and it says to treat unlisted statuses as false and not to infer benefit receipt. That gives 0, the engine's value. The derivation narrative wrongly says there is "no indication of qualifying disability," but the result still matches the law, because being disabled does not by itself create Medicare entitlement. The 19-model consensus of 1 treats the disability flag alone as enough, which the statute does not support.

claude_engine_step_at_issue: The engine allowed the Colorado sales tax refund ($19, computed from MAGI of $4,625.40) for tax year 2026. It applied the tax year 2025 refund table without the statutory condition that FY 2025-26 revenue exceed the TABOR/Referendum C cap. That condition was not met: it was projected unmet before the freeze and certified unmet in September 2026.
claude_summary: For tax year 2026, Colorado law (C.R.S. 39-22-2003) allows the state sales tax refund only if there were excess state revenues for the fiscal year ending in that tax year, which is FY 2025-26. Every official projection before the freeze, including the June 2026 Legislative Council Staff forecast, had FY 2025-26 revenue $424.9M below the Referendum C cap, with no refund obligation, so that refund is $0. The head is 66 and childless, so no federal EITC means no CO EITC, and there is no CO CTC, FATC, senior housing credit or other refundable credit. The engine's $19 is all sales tax refund. It is the published tax year 2025 lowest-tier single-filer amount carried into 2026, an amount 2026 law does not support. The law gives $0, which matches the consensus.

Michigan's homestead property tax credit gives a renter credit for 23% of gross rent (MCL 206.520(2)). For a non-senior, the credit is 60% of the amount by which that exceeds 3.2% of total household resources (MCL 206.522(1)). Any amount above tax liability is paid out (MCL 206.520(3)). Here that is 0.23 × $10,560 = $2,428.80, minus 0.032 × $36,276 = $1,160.83, which leaves $1,267.97; 60% of that is $760.78. The Michigan EITC (30% of the federal EITC) is $0, because a childless filer at $36,276 gets no federal EITC. The engine got $760.79 from the same steps. Its narrative wrongly calls the $1,267.98 excess an 'exemption', but the output matches the law. Stage 1 stands. The consensus answer of $0 leaves out the renter's refundable homestead credit.

Under Idaho Code § 63-3024A, each full-year resident who files gets a food tax credit (formerly the grocery credit) of $155 per personal exemption "for tax year 2025 and each year thereafter." Any part of the credit that exceeds the tax due is paid as a refund. The credit has no income limit. It is prorated only for months in which the filer received SNAP, and none is listed here. The engine counted $155 for one person over 12 qualifying months, which matches the statute. The 0 consensus wrongly assumed the credit is nonrefundable or income-limited, and stage 1 was right.

Federal WIC law limits the program to pregnant, postpartum and breastfeeding women, infants, and children under 5. The Head is 40 and the prompt lists none of those statuses. By the prompt's rules, unlisted statuses count as false. The youngest child is 2, so the Head cannot be postpartum (up to 6 months) or breastfeeding (up to 1 year postpartum). The engine found the Head not eligible and Child 2 eligible, which matches the law. "Receives wic" records benefit receipt, most naturally on behalf of Child 2. It does not establish the Head's eligibility category. The reference of 0 holds, and stage 1 stands.

The SNAP household is the three listed people. Their only income is $17,100 of self-employment earnings, or $1,425 a month. Under 7 CFR 273.10(e)(1) the 20% earned-income deduction ($285) and the FY2026 standard deduction ($209) leave net income of $931. Thirty percent of that is $279.30, which must be rounded to a whole dollar under 273.10(e)(2)(ii)(A), so the allotment is $785 − $280 = $505 a month, or $6,060 a year. The engine follows exactly these steps and uses the FY2026 amounts published before the freeze for all 12 months, which matches stage 1. The consensus of $6,068.40 leaves out the required whole-dollar rounding.

Under N.J.S.A. 54A:4-7, a New Jersey resident aged 18 or older with no qualifying child can claim the NJ EITC when age is the only reason they cannot take the federal credit. For these filers the credit is "predicated on the federal maximum amount for taxpayers with no qualifying child." The Division of Taxation treats that as a fixed amount set each year: $260 for 2025, which is 40% × $649. For 2026, Rev. Proc. 2025-32 sets the federal maximum at $664, so the credit is 40% × $664 = $265.60. That matches the engine's output. The engine narrative's mention of a phase-in to $308.55 that is then 'reduced' misdescribes how it got there, but the final value is the statutory fixed amount. The consensus of 0 wrongly applies the federal 25–64 age limit to the NJ credit.

The $33.20 reference is correct: it is Louisiana's refundable earned income credit, 5% of the federal EITC. Under IRC §32, the joint return qualifies for the no-qualifying-children EITC because the 43-year-old head meets the 25–64 age test, which either spouse can satisfy. Earned income from self-employment (about $9,665) is above the 2026 earned income amount of $8,680, and AGI is below the $18,140 joint phase-out threshold, so the federal EITC is the $664 maximum. R.S. 47:297.8 sets the Louisiana credit at 5% for 2019–2030 and refunds any excess over tax, giving $33.20. The engine's derivation matches this, as does stage 1. The 2025 bills to repeal the credit (SB 149, HB 642) or raise it to 10% (HB 133) all stayed in committee, and the statute's history still ends with Acts 2021, No. 453. The 25 models that answered $0 wrongly thought Louisiana has no refundable EITC, no income tax, or that the 20-year-old spouse disqualifies the couple.

claude_stage1_error: Stage 1's conclusion stands: the law supports the reference, not $0. My independent answer ($7.96) differs from stage 1's ($8) only by rounding convention. Stage 1 used the IRC § 32(f) table midpoint ($40 federal EITC, so $8.00). The 2026 EIC table had not been published by the 2026-07-03 freeze, so the only pre-freeze way to get the amount is the § 32(a) formula ($39.78, so $7.96). This is not a substantive error.
claude_summary: Va. Code § 58.1-339.8(B)(3)(b), checked again, gives a refundable credit equal to 20% of the federal § 32 EITC for taxable years from January 1, 2025 through before January 1, 2027, so it applies to 2026. The head is 40, single, has no children and has no investment income. They get a federal EITC of 7.65% × $520 = $39.78, still in the phase-in. Virginia tax is $0, so the refundable option is the right one. The engine took 20% × $39.78 = $7.956, which matches the law. The 25-model consensus of $0 is wrong: the refundable credit did not expire before 2026, and childless EITC phases in from the first dollar earned.

The reference of $288 holds. The household is one disabled person, an SSDI recipient, with gross income of about $2,146 a month. That is below 200% of poverty (about $2,608), so Michigan's broad-based categorical eligibility applies (BEM 213), and under 7 CFR 273.9(a) the household need not meet the gross or net income limits, and no asset test applies. With no shelter costs, 30% of net income (about $527 with the engine's $1,755 net income) exceeds the $298 maximum allotment, so the computed benefit is $0. But eligible one-person households get the minimum benefit, which is $24 a month in FY2026, so $24 × 12 = $288. The consensus answer of $0 comes from applying a net income limit, a 130% gross income limit, or an asset limit that categorically eligible households do not face.

Head is 62, so Medicare by age (65 or older) does not apply. Under 42 U.S.C. 426(b), a person under 65 qualifies only after 24 calendar months of entitlement to Social Security or railroad disability benefits, or through ESRD or ALS. Being disabled does not qualify anyone by itself. The prompt lists no Social Security disability income, says not to infer benefit receipt, and lists no ESRD or ALS, so the law gives 0. That matches the engine's output. The engine narrative wrongly says there is "no indication of disability" (the Head is listed as disabled), but correcting that does not change the result. The 15-model cluster wrongly treated a disability flag as enough on its own.

The reference of $465 holds. Idaho Code § 63-3024A, as amended by 2025 ch. 56, sets the food tax (grocery) credit at $155 for each taxpayer, spouse and dependent "for tax year 2025 and each year thereafter." The credit has no income limit, and any unused amount is paid as a refund, so it is refundable. The household has 3 people (the head and 2 dependent children), all eligible for 12 months, which gives 3 × $155 = $465. That is exactly what the engine computed. The cluster answer of 0 wrongly assumes the credit is nonrefundable or phases out at high income, and stage 1 correctly reached $465.

The law gives the same result as the engine. Monthly gross income is $1,511: SSDI of $630 plus the couple's SSI of $881, which is $1,491 minus ($630 minus the $20 exclusion). Arizona's $145 Standard Medical Deduction applies because the disabled household's medical costs are over $35. With the FY2026 standard deduction of $209, net income is $1,157. Thirty percent of that, rounded up, is $348, so the benefit is $546 − $348 = $198 a month, or $2,376 a year. The engine's derivation matches each of these steps, and stage 1 independently reached $2,376. The consensus figure of $1,956 used the $26 actual-cost medical deduction instead of Arizona's $145 SMD. The FY2027 figures ($562 maximum, $217 standard deduction, $160 SMD) take effect 10/1/2026, but they were published after the 2026-07-03 freeze, so frozen law uses the FY2026 values for all 12 months.

Under A.R.S. § 43-1072.01, the credit for increased excise taxes is $25 for each resident person with an exemption, up to $100 per household. A married couple qualifies with federal AGI of $25,000 or less, and the statute refunds any amount above tax due. This couple's only income is $7,560 of SSDI, which is not taxable under IRC § 86, so AGI is $0 and they get 2 × $25 = $50, all refunded. The engine credited exactly that $50 for a joint return with 2 people, so the reference holds. The $0 consensus wrongly assumes a refundable credit needs earned income or tax liability, and stage 1 stands.

claude_engine_step_at_issue: New York's child and dependent care credit is $360: 60% of the federal credit (20% of $3,000). This is the pre-2026 § 606(c)(1) computation, which L.2026 ch.59 limited to tax years beginning before 2026-01-01 and replaced with the § 606(c-2) credit on qualifying expenses.
claude_summary: Under the law in force for 2026, this household gets about $1,188 in refundable NY credits. The first part is the Empire State Child Credit of $307: $1,000 for a child aged three or younger, less 42 × $16.50 for federal AGI above $75,000. The second part is the new refundable NY child and dependent care credit of about $881 under Tax Law § 606(c-2), added by L.2026 ch.59 Part A and signed 2026-05-28: $3,000 of expenses × (55% − 0.00025 points per dollar of NY AGI above $15,000) ≈ 29.35%. The engine's ESCC is correct. For child care, though, it applied the old § 606(c) credit (60% of the federal credit, $360), which by its own terms now covers only tax years beginning before 2026. So the $667 reference rests on a repealed rule.

Pennsylvania taxes only the $1,675 of interest, at 3.07%, which gives $51.42 before credits. Social Security survivor benefits are not a PA taxable income class. The pension, 401(k) and IRA distributions to a 67-year-old retiree are excluded as old-age or retirement benefits. PA Tax Forgiveness (Schedule SP) is a nonrefundable credit, and its eligibility (poverty) income leaves out both retirement benefits and Social Security, per the statute and PA DOR. Eligibility income is therefore $1,675, under the $6,500 single threshold for 100% forgiveness, so the tax is $0. That matches the engine. The consensus of $51.42 leaves out Tax Forgiveness, apparently assuming Social Security or retirement income counts toward eligibility, which the law does not support.

California Education Code §49501.5(a) has applied since the 2022-23 school year. It requires public schools to give every pupil who asks a free breakfast and a free lunch each school day, whatever the family's income or federal eligibility. The household's 9-year-old is of school age, so the household gets positive free school meal support even though its roughly $166k income puts it far above the federal 130% and 185% cutoffs. The engine set the meal tier to FREE under California's universal program and returned $1,130.96 a year. That positive amount matches both the law and the output definition ("whether PolicyEngine returns positive annual free school meal support"). The consensus answer of 0 applied only the federal income test and missed California's universal-meals mandate.

The unit is the disabled head and two children, so its size is 3. The head is not an SSI recipient because the $2,800 bank balance is over the $2,000 SSI limit. The vehicle is excluded, which leaves countable resources of $2,800, under Montana's $3,000 limit. Net countable earnings are ($492.92 − $200) × 0.75 = $219.69 a month. That is far below the $1,465 GMI and $792 net income standards. The payment is the $725 payment standard minus $219.69, or about $505 a month and $6,064 a year. The engine's $6,064.96 matches this to within about $1, which is a rounding difference. The consensus answer of $0 depends on wrong asset limits, a made-up SSI receipt, or the belief that the program is not modeled.

The household is one person, age 85 and disabled, with monthly gross income of $2,581.83. That is just under Wisconsin's FY2026 200% FPL limit of $2,610, so the household is broad-based categorically eligible and no net income test applies. Net income is roughly $2,000–$2,200 a month, so 30% of it is far above the $298 one-person maximum and the computed benefit is $0. As an eligible one-person household it gets the $24 minimum instead: $24 × 12 = $288. The engine reaches the same result. Its net income ($2,036) differs from stage 1's ($2,214), but either figure gives the minimum benefit. The FY2027 $25 minimum comes from a USDA memo dated 2026-08-21, after the freeze, so $24 is the correct amount for Oct–Dec under frozen law. The consensus answer of $0 applies only the regular elderly/disabled 100% FPL net income test and misses Wisconsin's broad-based categorical eligibility (BBCE).

claude_stage1_error: Stage 1 stands in substance. One small arithmetic slip: 7.65% × $5,923 is $453.11, not $453.10. This does not change the result. The engine's $453.096 comes from the ratio $664/$8,680 and is within about a cent of the statutory figure; the IRS table gives $453.
claude_summary: The Head is 31, files single and has no qualifying children, so the only refundable credit they can claim is the EITC for a worker with no qualifying child. Earned income is the $5,923 of gross wages. AGI is $4,843: wages plus $1,920 of farm rent, less the capital loss limited to $3,000. Disqualified investment income is $1,920, under the $12,200 limit. The larger of AGI and earned income is below the $10,860 phaseout threshold, so the credit is the full phase-in amount: 7.65% × $5,923 ≈ $453.11. The engine's $453.096 uses an effective rate of $664/$8,680 (7.6498%), which differs from the statute by about a cent; the IRS EIC Table gives $453. The 0 cluster wrongly treats the ESI premiums as pre-tax pay reductions or adds nontaxable assistance to AGI. Neither reading fits the stated facts.

Alabama does not tax the $18,708 of Social Security. It does tax federally tax-exempt interest unless the bonds were issued by Alabama or one of its local governments (§ 40-18-14; r. 810-3-14-.02). The prompt names no issuer and says to treat unlisted facts as false, so the $4,734 counts as Alabama income. Alabama taxable income is then $4,734 − $3,000 standard deduction − $1,500 personal exemption = $234, taxed at 2%, which gives $4.68. The engine took exactly these steps. It also assumed medical expenses of $2,584.80, apparently by adding Medicare Part B premiums the prompt never listed. That changes nothing, because itemizing (about $2,600) still comes out below the $3,000 standard deduction. Most of the models answering 0 assumed Alabama exempts all federally tax-exempt interest, which is wrong. Stage 1 stands. One of its sources, an Alabama Department of Revenue FAQ, actually covers the financial institution excise tax, but its conclusion rests on the statute and the regulation.

From tax year 2025, NY Tax Law §606(e), as amended by Part RR of Chapter 59 of the Laws of 2025, tests the real property tax credit against federal AGI instead of household gross income. The head's federal AGI is $0, because $2,800 of Social Security is below the IRC §86 base amount. The head is a full-year resident aged 74 who paid $1,634 of property tax. The home's market value isn't listed, so the prompt's convention treats it as $0, which is under the $85,000 limit. The refundable credit is therefore the $375 maximum for filers 65 or older. No other NY refundable credit applies, and no 2026 change was found, so the engine's $375 matches the law and stage 1. The cluster answering $0 missed the IT-214 credit.

Child 1 is 14 and the household's MAGI is about 169–192% FPL, so Child 1 meets FAMIS's age and income tests (above the Medicaid limit, at or below 200% FPL plus the 5% disregard). But federal CHIP law and Virginia's FAMIS rule exclude any child covered under a group health plan, and the stated facts say Child 1 has employer-sponsored insurance all year. The engine returns 0. Its narrative vaguely blames "age or categorical requirements"; the categorical bar is the existing group coverage. That matches the law, so stage 1 stands. The 15 models that answered 1 checked only income and age.

Under federal CHIP law and Virginia's FAMIS rule, a child covered by a group health plan cannot be a targeted low-income child. Child 2 'has employer-sponsored insurance', and the prompt holds that coverage constant all year, so Child 2 is not CHIP/FAMIS-eligible. The answer is 0, which matches the reference. On income alone Child 2 would pass: MAGI is about $52,569, or about 192% of the 2026 FPL of $27,320, under the 200% limit plus the 5% disregard. The 15-model consensus applied only that income test and missed the uninsured requirement. The engine's narrative credits the 0 to income, which may be a misdescription, but it does not change the output the law requires on these facts. Stage 1 stands.

Head is 53, so the age route under 42 U.S.C. 426(a) does not apply. A person under 65 qualifies for Medicare only after 24 months of entitlement to Title II Social Security or Railroad Retirement disability benefits (§ 426(b); 42 CFR 406.12), or through ESRD or ALS. The prompt lists a generic "disability benefits" amount. It does not say the benefit is SSDI, gives no months of entitlement, and lists no ESRD or ALS. Under the prompt's rule, unlisted numeric inputs are 0 and unlisted statuses are false. The engine therefore correctly returns 0, and the consensus of 1 rests on two unlisted assumptions: that the benefit is SSDI and that the 24-month wait has passed.

Under 7 CFR 271.2 and 7 U.S.C. 2012(j), a 53-year-old counts as a disabled member only if they receive certain listed benefits: SSI, Social Security Act Title I/II/X/XIV/XVI disability payments, permanent governmental disability retirement, VA total disability, and similar. A general "is disabled" flag plus unnamed "disability benefits" does not meet that test. The prompt also says not to infer unlisted benefit receipt. Head's wages of about $2,139 a month are above the 2026 SSDI earnings limit of $1,690, so Social Security disability is implausible. That leaves Head subject to the gross income test. Gross income of $3,325.75 a month exceeds the FY2026 limit of $1,696 for one person (7 CFR 273.9(a)), so SNAP is $0, which matches the engine. The consensus of $3,576 assumes Head is SNAP-disabled. Even then it needs the $8,389 employer insurance premiums counted as out-of-pocket, or the $2,200 premiums counted twice, to bring net income to zero.

claude_engine_step_at_issue: The engine starts from the tax unit's IRS gross income of $100,002 (head and spouse only) to get pa_total_taxable_income. It drops the dependent child's $45,000 of wages and models no separate PA-40 for the child, so the child's $1,381.50 of PA tax is missing from state_income_tax_before_refundable_credits.
claude_summary: Pennsylvania taxes each dollar of income at a flat 3.07%, with no deductions or exemptions. The parents' joint PA-40 covers $100,002 of income, for $3,070.06 of tax. The 16-year-old has $45,000 of wages and must file a separate PA-40, owing $1,381.50. Tax forgiveness is $0 at these incomes, so the household owes $4,451.56 in total. The engine's $3,070.06 is correct for the parents' return, but it treats the child only as a dependent and never computes the child's own required return. The output definition does not limit itself to one return, and the prompt says to assume filing where required, so the engine leaves out a return the definition covers. The output should be excluded, or recomputed to include the child's return.
